# Data {#sec-data}

Parent-reported vocabulary checklists record a subset of the words a child knows, speaks or signs.

Lexical items - a subset of total words known.

## Measures

All studies assessed vocabulary using word checklists. Where respondent information was available, the checklist was completed by a parent or other caregiver, who recorded whether their child understood, said, signed or otherwise expressed each listed word. Parent-reported Communicative Development Inventory (CDI) scores have shown good validity for children with Down syndrome [@millerValidityParentReport1995]. Each score counts only the words on its checklist, not every word the child knows.

Most instruments were versions or adaptations of the MacArthur-Bates CDI [@fensonMacArthurCommunicativeDevelopment1993; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023]: the 396-item Words and Gestures form, the 680-item Words and Sentences form, the 416-item British Oxford CDI [@hamiltonInfantVocabularyDevelopment2000], Italian forms of 408 or 670 items, the 651-item Spanish CDI-Down, a 675-item New Zealand CDI and a 674-item Reading CDI. The three DSE Vocabulary Checklists hold 810 printed words, plus blank spaces for a child's own name and other personal words, so the highest achievable count is a little above 810. Some studies used only the first one or two checklists, and several forms were adapted to record signing or symbolic gestures [@galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011].

Results were converted into common measures of words understood, spoken and, where available, signed. A word could be both spoken and signed, so these counts were not simply added together. Every count was then scored against the 810-word DSE inventory as a common reference, rather than converted to a percentage or scaled up to match it. Each form's own maximum was also retained to identify impossible values and possible ceiling effects. This assumes that shorter early-vocabulary forms mainly omit words learned later.

### Signing measures

Sources record signing in different ways, and the signing fields are harmonised before fitting. `uk_01` records sign-only words and cannot identify total signed vocabulary from its aggregate data, so its understood and spoken values are retained while its signing values are masked in the primary signing analyses (VG14, VG15 and VG17); an explicit sensitivity analysis reintroduces it rather than pooling it silently with the comparable total-sign measures. The `uk_06` signing field was masked on the same principle while its construct was unverified, and was reinstated once the source confirmed the instrument: the standard DSE checklists, whose second column is completed for a word the child *understands and signs*, ticked for imitated as well as spontaneous signs. That is a total sign count, and the data agrees -- signed and spoken are each nested within understood on every uk_06 record, while their sum exceeds it on seven of eleven, which only overlapping per-word ticks can produce.

## Studies

We pool data from a variety of sources, including data collected by charities and research groups across multiple countries. The studies below are ordered by when their data were collected. For some sources the period is recorded only approximately, or in a companion report rather than the publication cited here, and for one it is not recorded at all.

### A study of vocabulary, signing and grammatical complexity in 218 children with Down syndrome (uk_01)

This study (Le Prevost, 2000, unpublished) collected data using the MacArthur Communicative Development Inventory (CDI), using both the Words and Gestures and Words and Sentences forms [@fensonMacArthurCommunicativeDevelopment1993; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023]. The data were collected through several research projects at The Sarah Duffen Centre, a joint initiative of the University of Portsmouth and Down Syndrome Education International (then the Portsmouth Down's Syndrome Trust). Parents were provided with the form appropriate for their child's age. In many instances, adapted versions were used. In addition to the standard "understands" and "understands and says" options, the adapted Words and Gestures forms added an option to indicate if the child "signs" the word. The adapted Words and Sentences forms (which usually only include "says") added "understands" and "signs" as options. The original report described 218 children aged between 1 and 9 years, including 102 girls and 116 boys. It stated that 154 participants completed Words and Sentences and 64 completed Words and Gestures. The families participating lived in the five closest counties to Portsmouth -- Hampshire, West Sussex, Surrey, Dorset and Wiltshire. The current project data contain 214 usable assessments grouped under 129 name-derived identifiers. Because children's names were the only available way to link repeated assessments, these identifiers should not be interpreted as a definitive count of distinct children.

### The development of vocabulary in Spanish children with Down syndrome: comprehension, production, and gestures (es_01)

This data was collected as part of a study on the development of vocabulary in Spanish children with Down syndrome [@galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011]. The participants included 186 children with Down syndrome aged 11 to 71 months. All children had a monolingual Spanish background. The participating families were contacted through early intervention units and Down syndrome parent associations from different cities in Spain (mainly in the South). The study used an adapted CDI form consisting of 651 words organised into 21 categories, with options to record "understands" and "understands and says". In addition, the form included a third column to assess the comprehension and production of gestures representing specific lexical items. Symbolic gestures were defined as those gestures that, when properly taught or spontaneously learnt, substitute specific lexical items (e.g., closing the hand with tight fingers and moving it towards the mouth to simulate "to eat"). The gesture column is therefore a per-word record of manual expression, taught signs and spontaneously learnt gestures alike, which the source does not separate; the authors use *signed* and *gestured* interchangeably, and parents were asked to mark only words "produced or signed referentially and spontaneously". The study's own typically developing comparison group, with no sign instruction reported, averaged 23.6 gestured words, so spontaneous symbolic gesture is captured. No other signing source in the pool records what its parents were told a sign is, so the column is read as this study's signed count on the same footing as the others, with one measurement caveat: after a validity check the authors eliminated eleven of the form's 21 word categories from the gesture data, and whether the totals supplied to us carry that elimination is being confirmed with the author. Collection dates are not reported; an earlier report from the same research programme described 66 children with Down syndrome in 2008 [@galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008].

### Vocabulary development in Italian children with Down syndrome (it_01)

These data came from two Italian studies of vocabulary development in children with Down syndrome, one longitudinal and one in which children were assessed once [@zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013]. The longitudinal study followed 18 children: ten from about two years for two years, and eight from about three years for one. A further 27 were selected from a language-development monitoring programme, nine at each of three developmental-age levels: about 18, 24 and 30 months. Collection dates are not reported. The monitoring programme these children attended was already running by early 2008, when a study of children at 36 months drawn from it was submitted for publication [@zampiniCommunicativeGesturesVocabulary2009].

Parents completed Il Primo Vocabolario del Bambino, the Italian version of the MacArthur CDI [@caselliPrimoVocabolarioBambino1995]. The 408-item Gesti e Parole form recorded words understood and spoken; the 670-item Parole e Frasi form recorded speech only, so comprehension scores come from the shorter form alone. The project file contains 54 children rather than the 45 described in the paper, including records collected beyond 48 months. The source of these additional records should be confirmed.

### DSE and Wates early-reading projects, United Kingdom (uk_02)

These data came from DSE and Wates Foundation language and early-reading projects conducted from approximately 2008 to 2012. The file combines three groups labelled edg2008, edg2009 and wates2010, with 136 assessments from 65 children aged 19 to 56 months. They are not separate samples: all 28 children in edg2009 also appear in edg2008, and nine of the 40 in wates2010 appear in the earlier groups. How families were invited, and the inclusion criteria, are not recorded.

The records contain either DSE Vocabulary Checklists or an Oxford CDI, 96 and 40 respectively; both recorded words understood and words expressed through speech only, sign only, or both. The available files do not identify who completed every form. The Oxford form used in wates2010 survives as a word-by-word file: 416 printed words in 19 categories, with 25 blank spaces for additional words, completed between January and May 2010.

### Reading and Language Intervention trial, United Kingdom (uk_06)

These data came from the Reading and Language Intervention trial reported by @burgoyneEfficacyReadingLanguage2012. The project was advertised in spring 2009 to parents of children with Down syndrome attending mainstream primary schools in Yorkshire and Hampshire. Children were eligible if they were in school Years 1 to 5. Fifty-seven children entered and were assigned either to begin the intervention immediately or to a waiting-list group, with assessments before intervention and after 20 and 40 weeks.

Parents completed all three DSE Vocabulary Checklists, covering 810 printed words and recording words understood, signed, imitated, used spontaneously and spoken clearly. The vocabulary file holds initial assessments for only 11 of the 25 children recruited in Hampshire, aged 60 to 115 months. No usable checklist data are present for the 32 children in the Yorkshire arm, suggesting that checklist data were collected or retained only in Hampshire. The spoken-clearly scores exist in the trial's original data file but were not included in the project vocabulary file.

### Word type and communication method in New Zealand children (nz_01)

These data came from children attending one early-intervention centre in a city on the South Island of New Zealand [@foster-cohenWordTypeModality2023]. The published study included 35 children with trisomy 21 aged 30 to 66 months, invited after attending the programme for at least 24 months and beginning to use five or more spoken or signed words. One child was excluded because cerebral palsy prevented communication by speech or sign. English was the main or only home language. The completions were collected between 2010 and 2017, as part of a larger study at the same centre [@foster-cohenVariationMorpholexical2023].

Mothers completed a 675-item New Zealand Words and Sentences CDI about every six months, recording for each word whether the child used speech only, sign only, both, or neither. The form measured expression but not understanding. The project data hold 111 assessments from 33 children, against 114 from 35 in the paper; the author-supplied workbook already contains the smaller totals, so these records were absent before the data were processed for this project.

### Mason-Apps longitudinal vocabulary data, United Kingdom (uk_04)

The Mason-Apps file holds 44 assessments from 18 children with Down syndrome aged 18 to 45 months, most assessed three times about six months apart. The numbers resemble the 18-child group reported by @mason-appsInfantsSyndromeShow2020, and some records may relate to the 14-child sample reported by @mason-appsLongitudinalPredictorsEarly2018. However, the ages and assessment patterns do not match either publication exactly, so the relationship should be confirmed. The file contains only children with Down syndrome. Collection dates are not reported in either paper; the doctoral thesis behind them was submitted in September 2013 [@mason-appsEarlyPredictorsLanguage2013].

In the associated studies, families were recruited through Down syndrome charities and University of Reading or local language-support groups. Because the file cannot be matched exactly to either publication, it is not certain that these recruitment routes describe all 18 children. Parents completed a Reading CDI at home before each visit, recording words understood, spoken and signed. Neither paper states how many words the form holds, and this project treats it as a 416-item British CDI. A later 674-item Reading CDI was used in PACT-DS, but this does not establish the length of the earlier form. Whether the signing column counted words the child also spoke is likewise unstated, and cannot be settled from the scores.

### Edgin/Wordbank vocabulary data, United States (us_01)

These data came from the Edgin files held in Wordbank, an open collection of CDI data [@frankWordbankOpenRepository2017]. The source covers children with Down syndrome and several comparison groups. @edgin2015sleep reported recruitment between 2012 and 2015 in Arizona and elsewhere in the United States, with exclusions for Down syndrome other than trisomy 21, birth before 36 weeks, cyanotic heart defects and a home language other than English. That study covers only part of these files, so it cannot describe the full sample.

Parents or caregivers completed the 396-item American-English Words and Gestures CDI or the 680-item Words and Sentences CDI. Words and Gestures recorded understanding and speech, Words and Sentences speech only; no signing measure was collected. After four entirely blank forms were removed -- two from children with Down syndrome -- the source files yielded 345 Down syndrome assessments from 122 children aged 5 to 173 months, 76 of whom completed both forms, linked by the study's own participant number. Further project checks reduced the analysed set, which spans 11 to 27 months.

### Joint-attention intervention, United Kingdom (uk_05)

These data came from Emily Seager's study of joint attention and language development [@seagerEarlyInterventionInfants2018]. Sixteen children with Down syndrome, aged 17 to 23 months at the start, were recruited through a University of Reading language-support group, local charities and the Down's Syndrome Association website. One child heard both English and German, with English the main language. None was already receiving a weekly joint-attention intervention. The recruitment materials set a closing date of 31 May 2016, and each child was then followed for twelve months.

Parents completed an adapted Reading CDI recording words understood, spoken and signed. Children then received a ten-week joint-attention intervention. The file holds 48 assessment records across three occasions, 46 with vocabulary scores, covering ages 17 to 36 months: the initial, six-month and twelve-month assessments.

### Cross-syndrome vocabulary study, United Kingdom (uk_03)

These data came from a study comparing children with Williams syndrome, Down syndrome, fragile X syndrome and typical development, each assessed once [@dsouzaExplainingComprehensionProduction2026]. The Down syndrome group was 27 children, 15 of them girls, aged approximately 12 to 39 months, all living in the United Kingdom with parents using only or mainly English. The paper does not report how participants were recruited or when the data were collected. A companion study of the same cohort was submitted for publication in January 2019 [@dsouzaAttentionalAbilitiesConstrain2020], which places these assessments well before the paper reporting them.

Parents completed the Oxford CDI, recording which words their child understood and produced. The paper describes this form as containing 418 words, whereas this project treats it as 416; no recorded count exceeds 416.

### See and Learn, Down Syndrome Ireland (ie_01)

These data were collected by Down Syndrome Ireland during the national See and Learn project, planned for the 2019/20 academic year [@downsyndromeirelandSeeLearnProject2019; @downsyndromeirelandAnnualReport2020]. Preschools delivered the See and Learn language programme in at least three ten-minute sessions a week for six months, and parents and educators attended regional training. Parents completed DSE Vocabulary Checklists at the beginning and end of the period.

The dataset holds 59 children aged 21 to 80 months at the first assessment, 46 of whom were assessed again six months later. The checklists recorded words understood, imitated and spoken. Checklists 1 and 2 were used initially, covering 460 printed words; the later assessment could include all three, covering 810. Preschool closures from March 2020 disrupted delivery and follow-up, so six-month changes cannot be attributed to See and Learn alone.

### Online language-through-music programme, Ireland (ie_02)

These data were collected during a 12-week online language-through-music programme delivered from mid-September to December 2022 [@frizelleFeasibilityOnlineLanguage2024]. Parents were invited through the Down Syndrome Ireland membership database, newsletter and social media. Children were eligible if they had Down syndrome, were exposed to English at home and would be aged 12 to 42 months during the programme; three younger children turned 12 months while it ran. Families were randomly assigned to watch the weekly video twice or five times a week.

Parents completed DSE Vocabulary Checklists 1 and 2 online before and after the programme, covering 460 printed words and recording words understood, signed, imitated, used spontaneously and spoken clearly. The published analysis included 68 children; the project data hold 67, with 116 assessments -- 67 before and 49 after. The group totals suggest that the missing child was in the higher-dose group. Later scores may reflect the intervention as well as ordinary development.

### Parent-delivered language programme trial, United Kingdom (uk_07)

These data were collected during a feasibility trial of PACT-DS -- Parents and Children Together, Down syndrome -- a parent-delivered early language teaching programme adapted for children with Down syndrome from an existing programme [@burgoyneProtocolRandomisedControlled2023]. A feasibility trial tests whether a full trial would be workable, not whether the programme works. Families were recruited by advertising through local parent support groups, speech and language therapy organisations and national Down syndrome organisations. Children were eligible if they had Down syndrome, were aged three to six years, lived within about 40 miles of Manchester or Reading, used at least ten English words or signs, had a minimum cognitive level of 18 months and had an English-speaking parent. Twins were excluded.

Thirty children took part, 15 in the intervention group and 15 on the waiting list. Parents completed a 674-item Reading CDI online before the programme, after the 30-week intervention and at follow-up, recording words understood and whether each was expressed through speech only, sign only, or both. The source holds 83 assessments from children aged 34 to 95 months; 82 are used, because one record reports more words produced than understood. The protocol planned a six-month follow-up, but the recorded ages give a median gap of four months between the second and third assessments.

### Single-assessment vocabulary data, United States (us_02)

These data hold one assessment from each of 26 children with Down syndrome aged 8 to 75 months. The file contains checklist totals for words understood and spoken, but does not record who completed the checklist. The collection dates, recruitment method, inclusion criteria and any publication describing this sample are all unrecorded.

The scores appear to come from the 396-item American-English Words and Gestures CDI, but this is inferred from their range rather than recorded: one child understood exactly 396 words and three others 390 or 391. One understanding score of 382 words at 16 months was treated as missing because it was considered unlikely to be correct; the spoken score was retained.

## Vocabulary by age {#sec-vocabulary-by-age}

Every observation in the pooled Down syndrome data, coloured by study, against the pooled interquartile band (25th–75th percentile) per 6-month age bin, drawn where a bin holds at least five observations. The scatter covers the pool's full age range deliberately: beyond about 72 months coverage rests on a couple of studies, which is why the results are reported to 72 months.

![Words understood by age in the pooled Down syndrome data, coloured by study, against the pooled interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/observations_age_understood_ds){#fig-obs-understood-ds .lightbox}

![Words spoken by age in the pooled Down syndrome data, coloured by study, against the pooled interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/observations_age_spoken_ds){#fig-obs-spoken-ds .lightbox}

The typically-developing Wordbank reference pool is too dense for a scatter — hundreds of administrations at each integer age — so its by-age view is the monthly distribution: one violin per month (density clipped to that month's observed range), with the pooled monthly median and interquartile band. Comprehension is measured only on the bivariate forms, so the understood panel ends where those forms do:

![Words understood by age in the typically-developing reference pool — monthly distributions with the pooled median and interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/violins_age_understood_td){#fig-obs-understood-td .lightbox}

![Words spoken by age in the typically-developing reference pool — monthly distributions with the pooled median and interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/violins_age_spoken_td){#fig-obs-spoken-td .lightbox}

## Repeated measures {#sec-repeated-measures}

Many children are measured more than once, and the within-child trajectories motivate the models' subject-level random effects. In the figures below each line joins one child's visits on one checklist form, drawn against the pooled median, mean and interquartile range for that age window (computed over all observations, single-visit children included). Lines are linked **within form only**: a child measured on two forms at one visit, or moved between forms, records counts on different item inventories, and joining those would draw measurement-scale changes as development. The Down syndrome figures cover the 8–72 month reporting window; individual trajectories fan widely around the pooled centre — same-age children span an order of magnitude in vocabulary, and individual slopes vary far more than the median slope.

![Words understood by age — repeated measures in the pooled Down syndrome data, coloured by study, against the pooled median (solid), mean (dashed) and interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/repeat_measures_age_understood_ds){#fig-rm-understood-ds .lightbox}

![Words spoken by age — repeated measures in the pooled Down syndrome data, coloured by study, against the pooled median (solid), mean (dashed) and interquartile band.](figures/descriptives/repeat_measures_age_spoken_ds){#fig-rm-spoken-ds .lightbox}

The same view of the typically-developing Wordbank reference pool, over its 8–30 month admission window (3-month bins; comprehension is measured only on the bivariate forms, so the understood panel ends where those forms do):

![Words understood by age — repeated measures in the typically-developing reference pool, coloured by dataset.](figures/descriptives/repeat_measures_age_understood_td){#fig-rm-understood-td .lightbox}

![Words spoken by age — repeated measures in the typically-developing reference pool, coloured by dataset.](figures/descriptives/repeat_measures_age_spoken_td){#fig-rm-spoken-td .lightbox}
